She was nineteen, and the boxes were plain white.

A Tufts student with celiac disease, a product for an audience the category had overlooked, and a belly band that was all the budget allowed. It ends up stocked in Las Vegas hotels.

GlutenFreedomForAll

Snack boxes · Julia’s Faves On-The-Go

Retail

Hotels and quick-service, nationwide

Julia’s Faves On-The-Go Snack Packs — her name, her face, and the allergen claim before anything else. Where it ended up.

The challenge

Julia was nineteen, a student at Tufts, and had celiac disease. She couldn’t find snacks she trusted while traveling, so she decided to make them — with a student’s budget and no distribution.

The category sells avoidance: free-from, no-gluten, warnings and exclusions. What she was actually selling was the opposite, to people the aisle had quietly overlooked — not a diet to accommodate, but the ordinary experience of eating something without having to ask.

And it had to work cold, on a shelf, to strangers.

The approach

Start at the size the business actually is. The first product was a plain white box, tissue paper, and a belly band carrying her logo. That was the whole package. Not a compromise — the correct answer for a founder with no capital and no proof yet. Money spent on cartons before anyone had bought one would have been money she didn’t have.

Sell belonging, not restriction. The line the business runs on — “where gluten-free is the norm” — reframes the category. Somewhere the question doesn’t come up.

Put the founder on the package. Her face, her handwriting, her diagnosis, first person: “When I was diagnosed with celiac disease, finding safe treats to eat was a challenge, especially when traveling.” A stranger in a hotel lobby learns why it exists before they read a single ingredient.

Then let it earn each upgrade. She sold boxes. Hotels in Las Vegas stocked them. Only then did it make sense to build printed cartons, a travel guide, a wholesale channel and a foundation — each one paid for by the stage before it.

The case first — market, burden of treatment, business model. The packaging came after the argument, not instead of it.
The personal layer — a note from Julia in every box, and a card asking what people actually thought. Direct marketing on no budget.
The direct-to-consumer side — subscription boxes, wholesale, and the shipper the whole thing arrived in.

On the shelf

The carton had to do three jobs in about three seconds: say gluten-free before anything else, say who made it, and look like a treat rather than a medical product. The green band carries the claim, the portrait carries the trust, and the inside panel carries her letter for whoever gets that far.

Flat to folded. The carton had to survive a shipper, a shelf and a counter, so the artwork was drawn on the dieline rather than fitted to it afterwards.

Beyond the box

A travel guide went out with the packs — practical tips for eating gluten-free on the road, from chef cards to airline meals. It cost nothing to include and did more for trust than any claim on the carton could.

“Traveling? Consider packing these foods.” The brand being useful rather than promotional.
On the counter at Ledo Pizza. Not a mockup — the product in an aisle it had to earn.

The outcome

Julia’s Faves On-The-Go Snack Packs reached Resorts World Hotels locations nationwide and quick-service retail, and a portion of profits funds celiac disease research through the GlutenFreedom Foundation.

One founder, from a white box on a dorm-room budget to printed cartons in hotel retail — every stage designed to fit the business she had at the time, not the one she hoped for.
